query: W is attractive for plasma-facing divertor components because of its high melting point, thermal resistance, low sputtering yield, and low tritium retention, but its relatively high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature limits use. CuCrZr provides favorable thermal conductivity as a heat sink but has a narrow operating-temperature range and is susceptible to irradiation embrittlement, requiring an intermediate layer that transfers heat efficiently while keeping both materials within suitable temperature ranges. Earlier HEA studies reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, thermal stability in Mo6.6Nb6Ni80Ta1.4Ti6, and favorable combinations of strength and ductility in NbTaTiV, HfNbTaTiZr, and TiVNbTa. Nevertheless, HEA performance can involve tradeoffs among strength, ductility, thermal stability, and phase constitution. TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC dendritic state combines about 800 MPa yield strength with approximately 40% strain, but its reported yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K are only 330 and 423 MPa, respectively, at 30% strain. Under the constraints of efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer, high-temperature mechanical stability, and compatibility with the limited operating ranges of both adjoining materials, what single intervention could improve the TiVNbTa intermediate material? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted change relative to the reported TiVNbTa baseline, temperature and loading boundaries, supporting evidence from the prior HEA results, and a controlled experiment that would falsify both the performance prediction and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled amount of molybdenum (Mo) into the TiVNbTa high‐entropy alloy (forming a Mo–Ti–V–Nb–Ta alloy) will improve its high‐temperature strength retention while maintaining its ductility, thereby better serving as an intermediate thermal transfer layer between tungsten and CuCrZr.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase BCC dendritic TiVNbTa alloy showing ~800 MPa yield strength and ~40% strain at room temperature but reduced yield (330 MPa) and compressive (423 MPa) strengths at 1273 K.
generation.intervention: Alloying modification via addition of a measured atomic fraction of Mo to the TiVNbTa composition to form a quinary alloy (Mo–Ti–V–Nb–Ta) while preserving the single-phase BCC structure.
generation.conditions: The modified alloy is processed under identical conditions as the baseline (e.g., similar casting/sintering to achieve dendritic BCC microstructure) and evaluated under high-temperature mechanical testing at around 1273 K (with 30% strain) as well as room-temperature tests. The application implies use as a thermal barrier intermediate layer between W and CuCrZr where both heat transfer efficiency and mechanical integrity in the respective temperature ranges are critical.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the single-phase BCC solid solution with refined dendritic morphology that is not compromised by secondary phase formation or segregation.
generation.mechanism: Mo addition is expected to enhance high-temperature strength retention by increasing overall lattice resistance to thermal softening and promoting a shift to edge dislocation-mediated plasticity, which is less thermally activated than screw dislocation motion. This should counteract the severe drop in yield strength at 1273 K seen in the baseline alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to pure TiVNbTa, the Mo–Ti–V–Nb–Ta alloy will exhibit higher yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K (improvement in the elevated-temperature regime), while maintaining or only modestly affecting the room-temperature ductility (around 40% strain near 800 MPa yield strength).
generation.baseline: TiVNbTa in its as-reported single-phase BCC state with ~800 MPa yield strength and ~40% strain at room temperature, but only 330 MPa yield and 423 MPa compressive strength at 1273 K.
generation.boundary: The material must operate as an interlayer that bridges the high-temperature W plasma-facing component and the low-temperature, irradiation-sensitive CuCrZr heat sink. Evaluation conditions are fixed to high-temperature mechanical testing at ~1273 K (and similar stress/strain conditions) and room-temperature performance tests, ensuring the modified alloy remains within the compatible operational ranges of both adjoining materials.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal Mo concentration and its quantitative effect on high-temperature strength are uncertain and will require systematic experimental calibration. There is also uncertainty regarding potential trade-offs in ductility or phase stability under prolonged thermal exposure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Mo-alloyed variants of the TiVNbTa alloy with increasing Mo content while keeping other processing parameters constant. Process each variant to achieve a single-phase BCC dendritic structure. Conduct mechanical tests at room temperature and at 1273 K (using both tensile and compressive setups) to measure yield strength, compressive strength, and ductility. Complement these tests with microstructural analyses (XRD, SEM/TEM) to verify phase stability.
measurements: Room-temperature yield strength and strain to failure
Yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K
Microstructural verification of single-phase BCC structure (absence of secondary phases)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-alloyed alloys do not show a statistically significant increase in high-temperature strengths compared to the baseline TiVNbTa (or exhibit undesired embrittlement or secondary phase formation that degrades ductility), then the hypothesis that Mo addition improves high-temperature performance via the proposed mechanism is falsified.

ABSTRACTOver 150 refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been proposed in the last decade. Early alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW still show an unparalleled yield strength of approximately 400 MPa at 1600°C. However, RHEAs with even elevated high-temperature strength are necessary in aerospace vehicles and nuclear reactors to cope with advanced technology in the future. Here, solid-solution strengthening calculation and melting point prediction are combined to design single-phase RHEA for attaining ultrahigh strength at 1600°C. The results show that Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW alloys after fully homogeneous treatment at 2100°C for 2 h reveal a homogenous body-centered cubic phase. HfMoNbTaW alloy exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, much higher than that of MoNbTaVW (477 MPa). It is found that a plateau of strength occurs from 800°C to 1200°C, which is important for raising the strength level of RHEAs at high temperatures. This strengthening mechanism is explained with the change of deformation mode from screw to edge dislocations, which contributes an edge-dislocation-induced strength.
